title: Σειρὰ χρυσείη
about: At dawn Zeus calls the gods to the top of Olympus and forbids any of them to help either side in the war: whoever goes will be struck down or flung into Tartarus. He challenges them to hang from a golden rope and try to drag him down from heaven; he could draw them all up, with earth and sea, and tie the rope to a crag of Olympus. The gods fall silent, and Athena answers that they will keep out of the fighting, but asks to give the Argives counsel so they do not all perish. Zeus smiles and says he did not mean it entirely, drives to Mount Ida, and sits looking down on Troy and the ships. Both armies arm and meet, and until midday the missiles fly. Then Zeus holds out his golden scales and weighs the death-spirits of Achaeans and Trojans; the Achaeans’ sink. He thunders from Ida, and the Achaeans are afraid; only Nestor stays, his horse struck by Paris’s arrow, and Hector’s chariot bears down on him until Diomedes calls to Odysseus to help.

sentences.t: Ἠὼς μὲν κροκόπεπλος ἐκίδνατο πᾶσαν ἐπ’ αἶαν,
sentences.l: Dawn, saffron-robed, for her part, was spreading herself over all the earth,
sentences.i: Dawn in her saffron robe was spreading over all the earth,
sentences.n: Book 8 opens at daybreak. Ἠώς ‘Dawn’ is the goddess, and κροκόπεπλος ‘saffron-robed’ is her stock epithet, built from κρόκος ‘saffron’ and πέπλος ‘robe’. ἐκίδνατο is the imperfect middle of κίδνημι ‘spread’, here ‘was spreading herself’; ἐπ’ … αἶαν is ἐπὶ αἶαν with the preposition elided, and αἶα is a poetic word for ‘earth’. μὲν answers the δέ that opens the next line, where Zeus takes over. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δὲ θεῶν ἀγορὴν ποιήσατο τερπικέραυνος
ἀκροτάτῃ κορυφῇ πολυδειράδος Οὐλύμποιο·
sentences.l:
and Zeus, delighting-in-the-thunderbolt, made an assembly of the gods
on the topmost peak of many-ridged Olympus;
sentences.i: while Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, held an assembly of the gods on the topmost peak of many-ridged Olympus;
sentences.n: The scene is Olympus. Ζεὺς δὲ … ποιήσατο is ‘and Zeus made’, the aorist middle of ποιέω; with ἀγορήν ‘assembly’ the middle is the idiom for ‘held an assembly’, and τερπικέραυνος ‘delighting in the thunderbolt’ (τέρπω ‘delight’, κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’) is put last in the line, away from the name it belongs to. Line 3 is a line the poem has already used for Zeus on his mountain: ἀκροτάτῃ is the superlative ‘topmost’, κορυφῇ ‘peak’, πολυδειράδος ‘many-ridged’ (δειράς ‘ridge’), and Οὐλύμποιο the epic genitive. The unit ends at the ano teleia at the end of line 3.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δέ σφ’ ἀγόρευε, θεοὶ δ’ ὑπὸ πάντες ἄκουον·
sentences.l: and he himself declared to them, and the gods, all, beneath listened;
sentences.i: he himself declared to them, and all the gods listened to him;
sentences.n: Zeus speaks and the gods listen. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Zeus; σφ’ is σφε ‘them’, accusative, with its vowel cut off. ἀγόρευε is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω, which for a public pronouncement we render ‘declare’. ὑπὸ … ἄκουον is a verb split from its preposition (tmesis): ὑπακούω ‘listen’, with ὑπό suggesting the hearer below the speaker, which the literal layer keeps as ‘beneath’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ πάντές τε θεοὶ πᾶσαί τε θέαιναι,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, all gods and all goddesses,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, all you gods and all you goddesses, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: Zeus opens his speech with the call for attention that begins speeches in assembly. κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with μευ the genitive ‘me’; πάντές τε θεοὶ πᾶσαί τε θέαιναι is ‘all gods and all goddesses’, θέαινα being the feminine of θεός. Line 6 is a standing line: ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may say’, and τά με θυμὸς … κελεύει is ‘what my heart bids me’, with θυμός ‘heart’ as the seat of impulse; its English is the same each time. Zeus’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
μήτέ τις οὖν θήλεια θεὸς τό γε μήτέ τις ἄρσην
πειράτω διακέρσαι ἐμὸν ἔπος,
sentences.l:
And let no female god, then, in this at least, nor any male,
try to cut across my word,
sentences.i: And let no goddess, then, nor any god either, at least in this, try to thwart my word,
sentences.n: The command is a ban on interference. μήτε … μήτε is ‘neither … nor’, each with τις ‘any’, so θήλεια θεός ‘female god’ and ἄρσην ‘male’ are the two classes forbidden; οὖν is ‘then’, and τό γε ‘in this, at least’. πειράτω is the third-person imperative of πειράω ‘let … try’, and it takes the aorist infinitive διακέρσαι of διακείρω, literally ‘cut through’, so ‘cut across, thwart’; ἐμὸν ἔπος is ‘my word’. The sentence runs on; the unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἅμα πάντες
αἰνεῖτ’, ὄφρα τάχιστα τελευτήσω τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.l:
but all together
applaud, so that I may most quickly accomplish these deeds.
sentences.i: but all of you together approve it, so that I may most quickly accomplish these deeds.
sentences.n: The positive order follows the ban. ἀλλ’ is ἀλλά ‘but’, ἅμα ‘together’, and αἰνεῖτ’ is the imperative αἰνεῖτε of αἰνέω ‘praise, assent to’. ὄφρα τάχιστα τελευτήσω is a purpose clause (ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive): τελευτάω ‘accomplish, bring to an end’, τάχιστα ‘most quickly’, and τάδε ἔργα ‘these deeds’, the work he has in mind.

sentences.t:
ὃν δ’ ἂν ἐγὼν ἀπάνευθε θεῶν ἐθέλοντα νοήσω
ἐλθόντ’ ἢ Τρώεσσιν ἀρηγέμεν ἢ Δαναοῖσι
πληγεὶς οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ἐλεύσεται Οὔλυμπον δέ·
sentences.i: Whichever god I perceive going of his own will, apart from the gods, to help either the Trojans or the Danaans, he will come to Olympus struck down, and in no good order;
sentences.n: The threat is stated in three lines of one sentence. ὃν … ἂν … νοήσω is ‘whomever I perceive’ (ἄν with the aorist subjunctive for a general case), with ἐθέλοντα ‘willing’ and ἐλθόντ’ ‘having gone’ agreeing with ὅν; ἀπάνευθε θεῶν is ‘apart from the gods’. ἀρηγέμεν is the infinitive of ἀρήγω ‘help’, with epic -μεν, and ἢ … ἢ ‘either … or’. Main clause: πληγείς (aorist passive participle of πλήσσω ‘struck’) … ἐλεύσεται ‘he will come’, the future of ἔρχομαι, and Οὔλυμπον δέ is ‘to Olympus’, with -δε of motion. οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ‘not in due order’ means in disgrace. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἤ μιν ἑλὼν ῥίψω ἐς Τάρταρον ἠερόεντα
τῆλε μάλ’, ἧχι βάθιστον ὑπὸ χθονός ἐστι βέρεθρον,
sentences.l:
or, taking him, I shall hurl him into misty Tartarus
very far, where the deepest pit is beneath the earth,
sentences.i: or I shall seize him and hurl him into misty Tartarus, very far away, where the deepest pit lies beneath the earth,
sentences.n: The second threat is Tartarus. ἤ ‘or’ opens it; μιν ‘him’ is the object of both ἑλών (aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘seizing, taking’) and ῥίψω (future of ῥίπτω ‘hurl’). Τάρταρον ἠερόεντα is ‘misty Tartarus’, ἠερόεις from ἀήρ ‘mist’. τῆλε μάλ’ is ‘very far’; ἧχι is the epic ‘where’; βάθιστον is the superlative of βαθύς ‘deep’, so ‘deepest’, and βέρεθρον is ‘pit’; ὑπὸ χθονός is ‘beneath the earth’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα σιδήρειαί τε πύλαι καὶ χάλκεος οὐδός,
τόσσον ἔνερθ’ Ἀΐδεω ὅσον οὐρανός ἐστ’ ἀπὸ γαίης·
sentences.l:
where are gates of iron and a threshold of bronze,
as far beneath Hades as heaven is from earth;
sentences.i: where there are gates of iron and a threshold of bronze, as far beneath Hades as heaven is from the earth;
sentences.n: The description of Tartarus continues. ἔνθα is ‘where’; σιδήρειαι ‘of iron’ (σίδηρος) agrees with πύλαι ‘gates’ and χάλκεος ‘of bronze’ with οὐδός ‘threshold’; there is no verb, and ‘are’ is understood. τόσσον … ὅσον is ‘as far … as’, with ἔνερθ’ ‘below’ taking the genitive Ἀΐδεω, the epic genitive of Ἀΐδης ‘Hades’ (the god, and so his realm); the second half is ὅσον οὐρανός ἐστ’ ἀπὸ γαίης ‘as heaven is from earth’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: γνώσετ’ ἔπειθ’ ὅσον εἰμὶ θεῶν κάρτιστος ἁπάντων.
sentences.l: then you will know how much the strongest of all the gods I am.
sentences.i: Then you will know how far I am the strongest of all the gods.
sentences.n: Zeus draws the conclusion. γνώσετ’ is γνώσετε, the second-person plural future of γιγνώσκω ‘know’; ἔπειτα ‘then’. ὅσον εἰμί is ‘how much I am’, ὅσον being an accusative of extent. θεῶν κάρτιστος ἁπάντων is ‘strongest of all the gods’, κάρτιστος being the superlative that goes with κρατερός ‘strong’.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε πειρήσασθε θεοὶ ἵνα εἴδετε πάντες·
sentences.l: But come, make trial, gods, that you may all know:
sentences.i: But come, make trial, gods, so that you may all know:
sentences.n: Zeus proposes a test. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is a fixed phrase ‘but come’ (the εἰ is part of the phrase, not ‘if’). πειρήσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of πειράω ‘make trial’; ἵνα εἴδετε is ‘so that you may know’, εἴδετε being the subjunctive of οἶδα with a short vowel (Attic εἰδῆτε). The test itself is in the next two lines. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
σειρὴν χρυσείην ἐξ οὐρανόθεν κρεμάσαντες
πάντές τ’ ἐξάπτεσθε θεοὶ πᾶσαί τε θέαιναι·
sentences.l:
a golden rope from heaven having hung down,
all of you fasten yourselves to it, gods and all goddesses;
sentences.i: hang a golden rope from heaven, and all of you, gods and goddesses alike, fasten yourselves to it;
sentences.n: The test begins with a rope. σειρὴν χρυσείην is ‘a golden rope’, ἐξ οὐρανόθεν ‘from heaven’ (-θεν ‘from’), and κρεμάσαντες is the aorist participle of κρεμάννυμι ‘hang’, here transitive: ‘having hung (it) down’, the first of the two acts. ἐξάπτεσθε is the imperative middle of ἐξάπτω, ‘fasten yourselves to it’, and πάντές τ’ … θεοὶ πᾶσαί τε θέαιναι repeats the address of line 5. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἂν ἐρύσαιτ’ ἐξ οὐρανόθεν πεδίον δὲ
Ζῆν’ ὕπατον μήστωρ’, οὐδ’ εἰ μάλα πολλὰ κάμοιτε.
sentences.l:
But you would not drag down from heaven to the plain
Zeus, the highest counsellor, not even if you toiled very much.
sentences.i: But you would never drag Zeus, the highest counsellor, down from heaven to the plain, however hard you toiled.
sentences.n: The outcome of the test: they cannot move him. ἂν ἐρύσαιτ’ is ἄν with the aorist optative of ἐρύω ‘drag’, ‘you would (not) drag’, and πεδίον δέ is ‘to the plain’ (-δε of motion). Ζῆν’ is Ζῆνα, the accusative of Ζεύς with its vowel cut off, and ὕπατον μήστωρ’ is ‘highest counsellor’: ὕπατος ‘highest’, and μήστωρα ‘counsellor, planner’, from the root of μήδομαι. οὐδ’ εἰ … κάμοιτε is ‘not even if you toiled’, the optative of κάμνω ‘toil, grow weary’, with πολλά as an adverb, ‘much’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ ἐγὼ πρόφρων ἐθέλοιμι ἐρύσσαι,
αὐτῇ κεν γαίῃ ἐρύσαιμ’ αὐτῇ τε θαλάσσῃ·
sentences.l:
But when I too, ready-minded, should wish to pull,
I would drag, with earth itself and with sea itself;
sentences.i: But whenever I, for my part, should wish to pull with a ready mind, I would drag you up, and earth itself and sea itself along with you;
sentences.n: Now the reverse: he could draw them all up. ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή … ἐθέλοιμι is ‘but when indeed I should wish’, the optative of ἐθέλω, and ἐρύσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐρύω with doubled σ for the metre. πρόφρων is ‘ready-minded’, as at the table’s other uses. αὐτῇ … γαίῃ … αὐτῇ … θαλάσσῃ are datives of accompaniment, ‘together with earth itself … with sea itself’; ἐρύσαιμ’ is ἐρύσαιμι with κεν, ‘I could drag’, and the Greek does not name what is dragged: the English supplies ‘you’, since the gods hang on the rope. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
σειρὴν μέν κεν ἔπειτα περὶ ῥίον Οὐλύμποιο
δησαίμην, τὰ δέ κ’ αὖτε μετήορα πάντα γένοιτο.
sentences.l:
The rope, then, around a crag of Olympus
I would bind, and all these things in turn would hang in mid-air.
sentences.i: Then I would tie the rope round a crag of Olympus, and all of it would be left hanging in mid-air.
sentences.n: The picture finishes with Zeus tying off the rope. σειρὴν μέν … δησαίμην is ‘the rope I would bind’, the aorist optative middle of δέω ‘bind’ with κεν, and ἔπειτα ‘then’; ῥίον is ‘crag’, a jutting rock, accusative after περί ‘round’. τὰ δέ κ’ αὖτε is ‘and these things in turn’, τά being the article as a pronoun, the gods, the earth and the sea together. μετήορα is ‘hanging in mid-air’ (the epic form of μετέωρος), and γένοιτο with κε is ‘would become’.

sentences.t: τόσσον ἐγὼ περί τ’ εἰμὶ θεῶν περί τ’ εἴμ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l: So much do I surpass the gods, and surpass men.”
sentences.i: So far do I surpass the gods, and surpass men.”
sentences.n: Zeus closes his boast. τόσσον is ‘so much’, with σσ for the metre. περί is an adverb ‘beyond’ here, taking the genitives θεῶν and ἀνθρώπων, so περί τ’ εἰμί … περί τ’ εἴμ’ is ‘I am beyond … and beyond’, ‘I surpass’; εἴμ’ is εἰμί with its vowel cut off. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ
μῦθον ἀγασσάμενοι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence
in admiration at the speech;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent, in admiration at his speech;
sentences.n: The gods are cowed. ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, elided, with the τ made θ before the rough breathing of οἱ. οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ‘and they then all’ are the gods, and ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is the set phrase ‘became still in silence’, with the same English each time. ἀγασσάμενοι is the aorist participle of ἀγάομαι (σσ for the metre), which means ‘wonder at’ or ‘be indignant at’; here it is the first, ‘in admiration’, as the reason in the next line makes clear. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 29.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ κρατερῶς ἀγόρευσεν.
sentences.l: for very strongly he spoke.
sentences.i: for he had spoken with great force.
sentences.n: The reason for their silence. μάλα γάρ ‘for very’ and κρατερῶς ‘strongly’, the adverb of κρατερός, go with ἀγόρευσεν, the aorist of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’, which the English puts in the past perfect because the speech is over.

sentences.t: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: But late indeed spoke among them the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: At last the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke among them:
sentences.n: Athena breaks the silence. ὀψέ ‘late’ marks how long it was before anyone dared; δὴ is ‘indeed’. μετέειπε is the epic form (with an extra ε) of μετεῖπε, the aorist of μετεῖπον ‘speak among’. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’, γλαυκῶπις being her stock epithet, whose exact sense (‘gleaming-eyed’, ‘grey-eyed’, ‘owl-eyed’) is disputed; the house rendering is ‘gleaming-eyed’.

sentences.t:
ὦ πάτερ ἡμέτερε Κρονίδη ὕπατε κρειόντων
εὖ νυ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν ὅ τοι σθένος οὐκ ἐπιεικτόν·
sentences.l:
“O father ours, son-of-Cronus, highest of rulers,
well indeed we too know that your strength is not yielding;
sentences.i: “Father of us all, son of Cronus, highest of those who rule, we too know very well that your strength is unyielding;
sentences.n: Athena answers Zeus with the address that line 31 has in the Odyssey; its English is kept. ὦ πάτερ ἡμέτερε ‘O father ours’ (ἡμέτερος ‘our’), Κρονίδη ‘son of Cronus’, ὕπατε κρειόντων ‘highest of rulers’, a vocative with the genitive plural of κρείων ‘ruler’. εὖ νυ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν is ‘well indeed we too know’: ἴδμεν is ἴσμεν, ‘we know’, from οἶδα. ὅ τοι σθένος οὐκ ἐπιεικτόν is ‘that your strength (is) not yielding’; ὅ is the conjunction ‘that’, τοι is ‘your’, and ἐπιεικτός ‘yielding’ has no verb to go with it. Athena’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔμπης Δαναῶν ὀλοφυρόμεθ’ αἰχμητάων,
οἵ κεν δὴ κακὸν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες ὄλωνται.
sentences.l:
but all the same we grieve for the Danaan spearmen,
who, having filled up an evil fate, shall perish.
sentences.i: but all the same we grieve for the Danaan spearmen, who will fill up an evil fate and perish.
sentences.n: She turns to the army. ἔμπης is ‘all the same’; ὀλοφυρόμεθ’ is the first-person plural of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament, grieve for’, with the object in the genitive Δαναῶν … αἰχμητάων (epic -άων for -ῶν), ‘the Danaan spearmen’. In the relative clause οἵ κεν δὴ … ὄλωνται is ‘who, indeed, shall perish’, ὄλωνται being the aorist subjunctive of ὄλλυμι with κε; κακὸν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες is ‘having filled up an evil fate’, οἶτος ‘fate, doom’, the aorist participle of ἀναπίμπλημι ‘fill up’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι πολέμου μὲν ἀφεξόμεθ’ ὡς σὺ κελεύεις·
sentences.l: But indeed from war we will hold off, as you bid;
sentences.i: But we will indeed keep away from the war, as you bid;
sentences.n: She gives way. ἀλλ’ ἤτοι is ‘but indeed’ (ἤτοι is one word as the edition prints it); ἀφεξόμεθ’ is the future middle of ἀπέχω with its vowel cut off, ‘we will hold ourselves off from’, with the genitive πολέμου ‘war’. ὡς σὺ κελεύεις is ‘as you bid’, and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: βουλὴν δ’ Ἀργείοις ὑποθησόμεθ’ ἥ τις ὀνήσει,
sentences.l: but a plan to the Argives we will suggest, such as will help,
sentences.i: but we will suggest to the Argives a plan that will help them,
sentences.n: What she offers instead. βουλὴν δ’ Ἀργείοις ὑποθησόμεθ’ is ‘but a plan to the Argives we will suggest’, ὑποθησόμεθα being the future middle of ὑποτίθημι ‘suggest, advise’ with its vowel cut off. ἥ τις ὀνήσει is ‘one that will somehow help’: ἥ is the relative ‘which’, τις ‘some’, and ὀνήσει the future of ὀνίνημι ‘benefit’.

sentences.t: ὡς μὴ πάντες ὄλωνται ὀδυσσαμένοιο τεοῖο.
sentences.l: so that not all may perish, you being angry.”
sentences.i: so that they may not all perish while you are angry.”
sentences.n: The purpose of her plan. ὡς μὴ … ὄλωνται is ‘so that not … may perish’, a negative purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive. ὀδυσσαμένοιο … τεοῖο is a genitive absolute, ‘you having been angry’: ὀδυσσάμενος is the aorist participle of ὀδύσσομαι ‘be angry’, and τεοῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘of you’. Athena’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἐπιμειδήσας προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her then smiling at addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: Then Zeus who gathers the clouds, smiling at her, spoke to her:
sentences.n: Zeus answers. τήν ‘her’ is Athena. ἐπιμειδήσας is the aorist participle of ἐπιμειδάω ‘smile at’, and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘addressed’; νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’, with νεφεληγερέτα the epic nominative in -α (compare ἱππότα). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: θάρσει Τριτογένεια φίλον τέκος·
sentences.l: “Take courage, Tritogeneia, dear child;
sentences.i: “Take courage, Tritogeneia, dear child;
sentences.n: θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. Τριτογένεια is a title of Athena whose meaning is not known: it has been taken as ‘Triton-born’, ‘born by the river or lake Triton’, and ‘third-born’, and the English leaves it as a name. φίλον τέκος is ‘dear child’, and the unit ends at the ano teleia. Zeus’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
οὔ νύ τι θυμῷ
πρόφρονι μυθέομαι, ἐθέλω δέ τοι ἤπιος εἶναι.
sentences.l:
not at all, you see, with a ready-minded heart
do I speak, and I wish to be kind to you.”
sentences.i: my heart is not wholly in what I say, and I wish to be kind to you.”
sentences.n: Zeus tells her he did not mean it all. οὔ νύ τι is ‘not at all, you see’, and θυμῷ πρόφρονι is ‘with a ready-minded heart’, so that the whole is ‘I do not speak with my whole heart’; the English gives the sense. μυθέομαι is ‘I speak’, first person present. ἐθέλω δέ τοι ἤπιος εἶναι is ‘and I wish to be kind to you’: τοι is ‘to you’, ἤπιος ‘kind, gentle’, and εἶναι the infinitive ‘to be’. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι τιτύσκετο χαλκόποδ’ ἵππω
ὠκυπέτα χρυσέῃσιν ἐθείρῃσιν κομόωντε,
sentences.l:
So having spoken, under the chariot he was making ready two bronze-footed horses,
swift-flying, with golden manes worn long,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and harnessed to his chariot his two bronze-hoofed horses, swift of flight, with their long golden manes,
sentences.n: Zeus drives out. ὄχεσφι is the old -φι form of the plural of ὄχος ‘chariot’ (the plural is used for a single car), so ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι is ‘beneath the chariot’, that is, under its yoke; and τιτύσκετο is the imperfect middle of τιτύσκομαι ‘make ready’. ἵππω is a dual, ‘two horses’, and so are the three words that agree with it: χαλκόποδε ‘bronze-footed’ (the form is χαλκόποδ’, elided), ὠκυπέτα ‘swift-flying’ (ὠκύς ‘swift’ + πέτομαι ‘fly’), and κομόωντε, the dual of the participle of κομάω ‘wear the hair long’. χρυσέῃσιν ἐθείρῃσιν is the dative ‘with golden manes’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: χρυσὸν δ’ αὐτὸς ἔδυνε περὶ χροΐ,
sentences.l: and gold himself he put on about his skin,
sentences.i: and he himself put gold on about his body,
sentences.n: He dresses for the drive. χρυσόν is ‘gold’, standing for golden clothing or armour (the Greek does not say which); αὐτός ‘himself’ is Zeus, and ἔδυνε is the imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’, with περὶ χροΐ ‘about his skin’, χροΐ being the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
γέντο δ’ ἱμάσθλην
χρυσείην εὔτυκτον,
sentences.l:
and took up a lash,
golden, well-made,
sentences.i: and took up a golden lash, well made,
sentences.n: γέντο is an aorist of a verb that has no present, ‘took up, grasped’, with δ’ ‘and’. ἱμάσθλην is ‘a lash’, χρυσείην ‘golden’ and εὔτυκτον ‘well-made’, both agreeing with it; the adjective χρυσείην is placed at the start of the next line, away from its noun.

sentences.t: ἑοῦ δ’ ἐπεβήσετο δίφρου,
sentences.l: and mounted his own chariot,
sentences.i: and mounted his chariot,
sentences.n: ἑοῦ is the reflexive possessive ‘his own’, agreeing with δίφρου ‘chariot’; ἐπεβήσετο is the aorist middle of ἐπιβαίνω, ‘mounted’, which takes a genitive. The ‘and’ δ’ joins this to the lash he has just taken, and the unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν·
sentences.l: and he whipped them to drive on;
sentences.i: he whipped them to drive them on;
sentences.n: μάστιξεν is the aorist of μαστίζω ‘whip’, with ἐλάαν the infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ (‘to drive on’); the horses, the dual of 41, are the object understood. The half-line also begins the line at Odyssey 3.484. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 45.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην
μεσσηγὺς γαίης τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος.
sentences.l:
and the two, not unwilling, flew
between earth and starry heaven.
sentences.i: and the pair flew, not unwilling, between earth and starry heaven.
sentences.n: τὼ ‘the two’, ἀέκοντε ‘unwilling’ and πετέσθην ‘flew’ are all duals, the Greek number for a pair (the two horses). οὐκ ἀέκοντε ‘not unwilling’ means eager. μεσσηγύς ‘between’ takes the genitives γαίης (Ionic -ης) τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος ‘of earth and of starry heaven’.

sentences.t:
Ἴδην δ’ ἵκανεν πολυπίδακα μητέρα θηρῶν
Γάργαρον,
sentences.l:
And to Ida he came, many-fountained, mother of wild beasts,
to Gargarus,
sentences.i: He came to Ida of many springs, mother of wild beasts, to Gargarus,
sentences.n: Zeus lands on the mountain that overlooks Troy. Ἴδην … ἵκανεν is ‘came to Ida’, ἵκανεν being the imperfect of ἱκάνω, and Ἴδην the accusative of Ἴδη, the mountain. πολυπίδακα ‘many-fountained’ is from πολύς and πίδαξ ‘spring’, and μητέρα θηρῶν ‘mother of wild beasts’, θήρ being a wild animal. Γάργαρον is Gargarus, one of Ida’s peaks, in apposition to Ἴδην. The unit ends at the comma, after the name.

sentences.t: ἔνθά τέ οἱ τέμενος βωμός τε θυήεις.
sentences.l: where for him is a precinct and a fragrant altar.
sentences.i: where he has his precinct and fragrant altar.
sentences.n: ἔνθά τέ is ‘where’, with the epic τε; οἱ is ‘for him’, the dative of the pronoun, so ‘he has’. τέμενος is ‘precinct’, a ground set apart for a god, and βωμός ‘altar’, with θυήεις ‘fragrant’ (from θύος ‘burnt offering, incense’). There is no verb: ‘is’ is understood.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἵππους ἔστησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε
λύσας ἐξ ὀχέων,
sentences.l:
There the horses he stopped, the father of men and of gods,
having loosed them from the chariot,
sentences.i: There the father of men and of gods stopped his horses, and loosed them from the chariot,
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ἔνθα ‘there’, and ἔστησε is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stop’; πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε is ‘the father of men and of gods’, Zeus without his name. λύσας ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘having loosed (them) from the chariot’, with ὀχέων the genitive plural of ὄχεα. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: κατὰ δ’ ἠέρα πουλὺν ἔχευεν.
sentences.l: and down a thick mist he poured.
sentences.i: and poured a thick mist down.
sentences.n: κατὰ … ἔχευεν is a verb split from its preposition (tmesis): καταχέω, aorist ‘poured down’. ἠέρα πουλύν is ‘thick mist’, πουλύς being the epic form of πολύς; the Greek does not say what he poured it over, and the English does not say either.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐν κορυφῇσι καθέζετο κύδεϊ γαίων
εἰσορόων Τρώων τε πόλιν καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
and he himself on the peaks sat down, exulting in glory,
looking on the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: He himself sat down on the peaks, exulting in his glory, looking out on the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: He takes his seat to watch the battle. αὐτὸς δ’ is ‘and he himself’, κορυφῇσι the epic dative plural ‘on the peaks’, and καθέζετο the imperfect of καθέζομαι ‘sat down’. κύδεϊ γαίων is a stock phrase, ‘exulting in glory’ (the dative of κῦδος, and γαίων is the participle of γαίω ‘exult’); εἰσορόων is the participle of εἰσοράω ‘look at’, with its vowels left uncontracted. Τρώων τε πόλιν καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρα δεῖπνον ἕλοντο κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ῥίμφα κατὰ κλισίας,
sentences.l:
And they then took their meal, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
nimbly, among the huts,
sentences.i: Meanwhile the long-haired Achaeans took their meal nimbly among the huts,
sentences.n: The scene moves to the two armies. οἳ δ’ ἄρα ‘and they then’ are the Achaeans, named at the end of the line with their stock epithet κάρη κομόωντες ‘long-haired-of-head’. δεῖπνον ἕλοντο is ‘took a meal’, ἕλοντο being the aorist middle of αἱρέω, as in δόρπον ἕλοντο. ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’ is an adverb, and κατὰ κλισίας ‘among the huts’ is the quarters along the ships. The unit ends at the comma. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ἀπὸ δ’ αὐτοῦ θωρήσσοντο.
sentences.l: and thereupon, on the spot, they armed themselves.
sentences.i: and then and there they armed themselves.
sentences.n: θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, ‘were arming themselves’. ἀπὸ δ’ αὐτοῦ is ‘and from (it), on the spot’: ἀπό is an adverb, whose exact force here is not certain, and αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘in that very place’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀνὰ πτόλιν ὁπλίζοντο
παυρότεροι·
sentences.l:
And the Trojans in turn, on the other side, throughout the city were making ready,
fewer in number;
sentences.i: While on the other side the Trojans, fewer in number, made ready throughout the city;
sentences.n: The Trojans prepare too. αὖθ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’, ἀνὰ πτόλιν ‘up and down the city’ (πτόλις is the epic form of πόλις), and ὁπλίζοντο ‘were making ready’, the imperfect middle of ὁπλίζω. παυρότεροι is the comparative of παῦρος ‘few’, ‘fewer’, and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
μέμασαν δὲ καὶ ὧς ὑσμῖνι μάχεσθαι
χρειοῖ ἀναγκαίῃ,
sentences.l:
but they were eager even so to fight in the battle,
by compelling need,
sentences.i: but even so they were eager to fight in the battle, under hard necessity,
sentences.n: μέμασαν is the third plural of the perfect μέμαα ‘be eager’, used as a past, ‘were eager’, and καὶ ὧς is ‘even so’, in spite of being fewer. ὑσμῖνι μάχεσθαι is ‘to fight in the battle’, the dative of ὑσμίνη. χρειοῖ ἀναγκαίῃ is ‘by compelling need’: χρειώ is ‘need’, and ἀναγκαίῃ ‘compelling, forced’, both datives of cause. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: πρό τε παίδων καὶ πρὸ γυναικῶν.
sentences.l: in front of children and in front of wives.
sentences.i: in defence of their children and their wives.
sentences.n: πρό is here ‘in front of’, and so ‘on behalf of’: the Trojans fight in front of their families, to shield them, which is why the English says ‘in defence of’. πρό τε παίδων καὶ πρὸ γυναικῶν has the genitives of παῖς ‘child’ and γυνή ‘wife, woman’.

sentences.t:
πᾶσαι δ’ ὠΐγνυντο πύλαι, ἐκ δ’ ἔσσυτο λαός,
πεζοί θ’ ἱππῆές τε·
sentences.l:
and all the gates were being opened, and out rushed the people,
both on foot and horsemen;
sentences.i: all the gates were opened, and out rushed the army, both on foot and mounted;
sentences.n: The Trojans march out. πᾶσαι … πύλαι ‘all the gates’ is plural; ὠΐγνυντο is the imperfect passive of οἴγνυμι ‘open’. ἐκ … ἔσσυτο is the aorist of σεύομαι ‘rush’, with ἐκ standing apart (tmesis), ‘rushed out’, and λαός ‘people, army’ is singular and takes a singular verb. πεζοί … ἱππῆες ‘men on foot and horsemen’ is a pair, with ἱππῆες the epic form of ἱππεῖς. These two lines are also 2.809–810. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 59.

sentences.t: πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει.
sentences.l: and a great din had risen.
sentences.i: and a great din rose.
sentences.n: πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδός is ‘and a great din’, and ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘had risen’, which in English reads as a plain past, ‘rose’. The half-line also stands at 2.810 and again at 63, where the longer unit it ends has its own wording.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐς χῶρον ἕνα ξυνιόντες ἵκοντο
σύν ῥ’ ἔβαλον ῥινούς, σὺν δ’ ἔγχεα καὶ μένε’ ἀνδρῶν
χαλκεοθωρήκων·
sentences.i: And when they had come together into one place, they dashed together their hide shields, their spears, and the might of men in bronze breastplates;
sentences.n: The armies meet. οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ‘and when indeed’ (ῥα = ἄρα) opens the clash. ξυνιόντες is the participle of ξύνειμι ‘come together’, and ἵκοντο is the aorist ‘reached’. σὺν … ἔβαλον is tmesis of συμβάλλω ‘dash together’, and σύν is repeated before ἔγχεα. ῥινούς are ‘hides’, that is, shields covered with hide; μένε’ is the elided plural of μένος ‘might’. χαλκεοθωρήκων ‘in bronze breastplates’ is a compound of χάλκεος ‘bronze’ and θώρηξ ‘breastplate’. These lines are also 4.446–448. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι
ἔπληντ’ ἀλλήλῃσι, πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει.
sentences.l:
and the bossed shields
were brought together with one another, and a great din had sprung up.
sentences.i: and the bossed shields clashed together, and a great din went up.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘and, but’. ὀμφαλόεσσαι ‘bossed’ describes shields with an ὀμφαλός, the central boss. ἔπληντ’ is the elided aorist ἔπληντο of πελάζω ‘bring near’, here passive, ‘were brought up against’ one another (ἀλλήλῃσι, a dative). The half-line πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει is the one that also ends 2.810 and line 59 above.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἅμ’ οἰμωγή τε καὶ εὐχωλὴ πέλεν ἀνδρῶν
ὀλλύντων τε καὶ ὀλλυμένων, ῥέε δ’ αἵματι γαῖα.
sentences.l:
There together were wailing and boasting of men
destroying and perishing, and flowed with blood the earth.
sentences.i: There together were the wailing and the boasting of men killing and being killed, and the earth ran with blood.
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ‘there’. ἅμ’ ‘together, at once’ goes with the pair οἰμωγή τε καὶ εὐχωλή: a cry of pain and a victor’s boast. πέλεν is the imperfect of πέλομαι ‘be, come to be’, without the augment. ἀνδρῶν is shared by both nouns and by the two participles ὀλλύντων and ὀλλυμένων, active ‘killing’ and passive ‘being killed’, from ὄλλυμι. ῥέε δ’ αἵματι γαῖα: αἵματι is a dative of means, ‘ran with blood’.

sentences.t: ὄφρα μὲν ἠὼς ἦν καὶ ἀέξετο ἱερὸν ἦμαρ,
sentences.l: As long as it was morning and the sacred day was growing,
sentences.i: For as long as it was morning and the sacred day was growing,
sentences.n: A new stage of the day. ὄφρα … τόφρα (the next line) is a pair, ‘as long as … for that time’. ἠώς here is the common noun ‘morning’ (not the goddess), with ἦν ‘was’; ἀέξετο is the imperfect passive of ἀέξω ‘make grow’, ‘was growing’, and ἱερὸν ἦμαρ is ‘the sacred day’, the poet’s fixed phrase. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: τόφρα μάλ’ ἀμφοτέρων βέλε’ ἥπτετο, πῖπτε δὲ λαός.
sentences.l: for that time the missiles of both sides took hold, and the people fell.
sentences.i: for that time the missiles of both sides struck home, and the troops fell.
sentences.n: τόφρα ‘for that time’ answers ὄφρα in the line before, and μάλ’ strengthens it. ἀμφοτέρων βέλε’ is ‘the missiles of both sides’, with βέλε’ the elided plural of βέλος ‘missile’. ἥπτετο is the imperfect middle of ἅπτω, ‘took hold’, that is, hit its mark; πῖπτε is the imperfect of πίπτω ‘fall’, and λαός is again the army.

sentences.t: ἦμος δ’ Ἠέλιος μέσον οὐρανὸν ἀμφιβεβήκει,
sentences.l: But when the Sun had bestridden the middle of heaven,
sentences.i: But when the Sun had reached the middle of heaven,
sentences.n: ἦμος is ‘when’. Ἠέλιος is ‘the Sun’, here the god, and μέσον οὐρανόν is ‘the middle of heaven’. ἀμφιβεβήκει is the pluperfect of ἀμφιβαίνω ‘stride about, bestride’, ‘had bestridden’; it is a past perfect used for ‘had come to’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε δὴ χρύσεια πατὴρ ἐτίταινε τάλαντα·
sentences.l: then indeed the father was holding out golden scales;
sentences.i: then the Father held out his golden scales;
sentences.n: καὶ τότε δή is ‘then indeed’. πατήρ is ‘the father’, that is Zeus, called by his title and not his name. ἐτίταινε is the imperfect of τιταίνω ‘stretch out’, ‘was holding out’, and χρύσεια τάλαντα is ‘golden scales’: τάλαντα in the plural is the balance itself (the singular is also a weight, ‘talent’). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει δύο κῆρε τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο
Τρώων θ’ ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων,
sentences.l:
and in them he placed two death-spirits of death that lays-at-length,
of the horse-taming Trojans and the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
sentences.i: and in them he put two spirits of death that lays men at length, of the Trojans, tamers of horses, and the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
sentences.n: What goes into the scales. ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει is ‘and he put in’, the imperfect of τίθημι. κῆρε is the dual of κήρ, a death-spirit, the lot of death that belongs to a man or an army, here two of them; τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο is ‘of death that lays men at length’, a stock phrase whose meaning is not known: τανηλεγής has been taken as ‘laying (men) at length’ and as ‘bringing long pain’, and the English follows the first. Τρώων θ’ ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων is ‘of the horse-taming Trojans and the bronze-shirted Achaeans’; the half-line also stands at 3.127. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: ἕλκε δὲ μέσσα λαβών·
sentences.l: and he drew them, taking them by the middle;
sentences.i: and taking hold of them in the middle he drew them up;
sentences.n: ἕλκε is the imperfect of ἕλκω ‘draw, lift’, and λαβών the aorist participle of λαμβάνω ‘take’. μέσσα is the neuter plural ‘by the middle’, here the middle of the balance. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ῥέπε δ’ αἴσιμον ἦμαρ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: and sank the fated day of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and the Achaeans’ fated day sank.
sentences.n: ῥέπε is the imperfect of ῥέπω ‘incline, sink’, the pan of the scales going down. αἴσιμον ἦμαρ is ‘the fated day’, αἴσιμος from αἶσα ‘fate’, so the day that is theirs by fate; the Achaeans’ pan is the one that sinks.

sentences.t:
αἳ μὲν Ἀχαιῶν κῆρες ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ
ἑζέσθην, Τρώων δὲ πρὸς οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἄερθεν·
sentences.l:
The death-spirits of the Achaeans on the earth, feeding many,
settled, and those of the Trojans toward broad heaven were lifted;
sentences.i: The Achaeans’ spirits of death settled on the earth that feeds so many, and the Trojans’ were lifted up toward broad heaven;
sentences.n: αἳ μὲν Ἀχαιῶν κῆρες is ‘the death-spirits of the Achaeans’, with αἳ the article as a pronoun; ἑζέσθην is the dual aorist of ἕζομαι, ‘settled, sat down’. Τρώων δέ has κῆρες understood, ‘and those of the Trojans’, and ἄερθεν is the aorist passive of ἀείρω ‘lift’, with -εν for -ησαν, ‘were lifted’. χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ is ‘the much-nourishing earth’ (the line is a stock ending), and οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘broad heaven’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐξ Ἴδης μεγάλ’ ἔκτυπε, δαιόμενον δὲ
ἧκε σέλας μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
and he himself from Ida crashed mightily, and a blazing
flash he sent among the people of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: he himself thundered mightily from Ida, and sent a blazing flash among the army of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: Zeus gives a sign. αὐτὸς δ’ is ‘and he himself’, ἐξ Ἴδης ‘from Ida’. ἔκτυπε is the aorist of κτυπέω ‘make a loud crash’, here ‘thundered’; μεγάλ’ is the adverb ‘mightily’. δαιόμενον … σέλας is ‘a blazing flash’, the participle of δαίομαι ‘blaze’ agreeing with σέλας ‘flash’. ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’. μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν is ‘among the army of the Achaeans’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 76.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ ἰδόντες
θάμβησαν, καὶ πάντας ὑπὸ χλωρὸν δέος εἷλεν.
sentences.l:
and they, having seen it,
were amazed, and from beneath pale fear took them all.
sentences.i: and when they saw it they were amazed, and pale fear seized them all.
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ ἰδόντες is ‘and they, having seen’, the aorist participle of ὁράω; θάμβησαν is the aorist of θαμβέω ‘be amazed’. χλωρὸν δέος is ‘pale fear’, χλωρός being a pale green or yellow, and ὑπὸ … εἷλεν is a verb split from its preposition (tmesis), the aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’, with ὑπό ‘from below’. The same phrase χλωρὸν δέος has the same English wherever it recurs.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὔτ’ Ἰδομενεὺς τλῆ μίμνειν οὔτ’ Ἀγαμέμνων,
οὔτε δύ’ Αἴαντες μενέτην θεράποντες Ἄρηος·
sentences.l:
Then neither Idomeneus endured to stay, nor Agamemnon,
nor did the two Ajaxes stay, attendants of Ares;
sentences.i: Then neither Idomeneus could bear to stay, nor Agamemnon, nor did the two Ajaxes, attendants of Ares, stand their ground;
sentences.n: The Achaean leaders flee. οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor … nor’; τλῆ is the aorist of τλάω ‘endure, bring oneself to’, with the infinitive μίμνειν ‘to stay’. δύ’ Αἴαντες is ‘the two Ajaxes’ (the plural names the pair), and μενέτην is the dual imperfect of μένω, ‘stayed’. θεράποντες Ἄρηος is ‘attendants of Ares’, as at 2.110. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Νέστωρ οἶος ἔμιμνε Γερήνιος οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν
οὔ τι ἑκών,
sentences.l:
Nestor alone remained, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans,
not at all willingly,
sentences.i: Nestor alone remained, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans, and not willingly,
sentences.n: Nestor stays, but not by choice. οἶος is ‘alone’, ἔμιμνε the imperfect of μίμνω (the poetic form of μένω) ‘remained’. Γερήνιος is his stock epithet, whose meaning is disputed (from Gerenia, or from γέρων ‘old man’), and so it stays a name; οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν is ‘warden of the Achaeans’, οὖρος being ‘guardian’. οὔ τι ἑκών is ‘not at all willingly’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἵππος ἐτείρετο, τὸν βάλεν ἰῷ
δῖος Ἀλέξανδρος Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο
sentences.l:
but his horse was being distressed, which with an arrow struck
heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen,
sentences.i: but his horse was in distress, struck by an arrow from heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἵππος ἐτείρετο is ‘but a horse was being distressed’, the imperfect passive of τείρω ‘wear down, distress’. τὸν βάλεν ἰῷ is ‘which he struck with an arrow’: τόν is ‘which’, βάλεν the aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’, and ἰῷ the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’ (the same word also means ‘poison’). The archer is δῖος Ἀλέξανδρος Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο, ‘heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen’, a line that is used for Paris at 3.329. The sentence continues; the unit ends at the end of line 82, with no stop.

sentences.t:
ἄκρην κὰκ κορυφήν, ὅθι τε πρῶται τρίχες ἵππων
κρανίῳ ἐμπεφύασι, μάλιστα δὲ καίριόν ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
on the topmost crown, where the first hairs of horses
grow on the skull, and where it is most deadly.
sentences.i: on the very top of its head, where the first hairs of horses grow on the skull, and where a wound is most deadly.
sentences.n: Where the arrow struck. ἄκρην κὰκ κορυφήν is ‘on the topmost crown’: κὰκ is κατά with the τ assimilated to the κ that follows, and κορυφή is ‘head-top, peak’. ὅθι τε is ‘where’; πρῶται τρίχες ἵππων is ‘the first hairs of horses’, those nearest the front of the head, and ἐμπεφύασι is the perfect of ἐμφύω ‘grow in’. κρανίῳ is ‘in the skull’, a dative of place. μάλιστα δὲ καίριόν ἐστιν is ‘and it is most deadly’, καίριος meaning ‘at the vital spot’.

sentences.t: ἀλγήσας δ’ ἀνέπαλτο, βέλος δ’ εἰς ἐγκέφαλον δῦ,
sentences.l: and in pain it leapt up, and the missile into the brain sank,
sentences.i: In pain it leapt up, and the arrow sank into its brain,
sentences.n: ἀλγήσας is the aorist participle of ἀλγέω ‘feel pain’; ἀνέπαλτο is the aorist of ἀναπάλλομαι ‘leap up’. βέλος is the missile, here the arrow of 81, and δῦ is ἔδυ, the aorist of δύω ‘sink in’. ἐγκέφαλον is the brain.

sentences.t: σὺν δ’ ἵππους ἐτάραξε κυλινδόμενος περὶ χαλκῷ.
sentences.l: and the horses it threw into confusion, rolling about the bronze.
sentences.i: and, writhing round the bronze point, it threw the horses into confusion.
sentences.n: σὺν … ἐτάραξε is a verb split from its preposition (tmesis): συνταράσσω, aorist ‘threw into confusion’. κυλινδόμενος is the participle of κυλίνδομαι ‘roll about’, here the wounded horse writhing; περὶ χαλκῷ is ‘around the bronze’, the arrowhead.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ὁ γέρων ἵπποιο παρηορίας ἀπέταμνε
φασγάνῳ ἀΐσσων,
sentences.l:
While the old man was cutting the traces of the horse
with his sword, darting at them,
sentences.i: While the old man, darting at them with his sword, was cutting the horse’s traces,
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ is ὄφρα ‘while’, ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, Nestor. ἀπέταμνε is the imperfect of ἀποτέμνω ‘cut off’; παρηορίαι is the rare word for the traces or side-straps of the outer horse of a team, and its exact meaning is not certain. φασγάνῳ is ‘with his sword’, a dative of means, and ἀΐσσων the participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, rush’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
τόφρ’ Ἕκτορος ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἦλθον ἀν’ ἰωχμὸν θρασὺν ἡνίοχον φορέοντες
Ἕκτορα·
sentences.i: meanwhile Hector’s swift horses came through the press of the fight, carrying their bold charioteer, Hector;
sentences.n: τόφρ’ is τόφρα ‘for that time, meanwhile’, answering ὄφρ’ in 87. Ἕκτορος ὠκέες ἵπποι is ‘Hector’s swift horses’, and ἦλθον ‘came’ is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. ἀν’ ἰωχμόν is ‘through the press’, ἰωχμός being a rare word for the rush of battle, whose exact sense is not certain. θρασὺν ἡνίοχον is ‘a bold charioteer’, ἡνίοχος ‘charioteer’ (the one who holds the reins), and φορέοντες is the participle of φορέω ‘carry’; Ἕκτορα, at the start of line 90, says who he is. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 90.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἔνθ’ ὁ γέρων ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὄλεσσεν
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.l:
and now there the old man would have lost his life,
if Diomedes, good at the war-cry, had not sharply noticed it;
sentences.i: And now there the old man would have lost his life, had not Diomedes, good at the war-cry, been quick to notice;
sentences.n: Nestor’s danger. καί νύ κεν … ὄλεσσεν is ‘and now … would have lost’, the unreal past: κεν with the aorist, and ἀπὸ … ὄλεσσεν is a verb split from its preposition (tmesis), ἀπόλλυμι ‘destroy, lose’, with θυμὸν ‘life’ as the house has it. εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε is the stock ‘if he had not sharply noticed’: νόησε is the aorist of νοέω ‘perceive’. βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης is ‘Diomedes, good at the war-cry’. The unit ends at the ano teleia at the end of line 91.

sentences.t: σμερδαλέον δ’ ἐβόησεν ἐποτρύνων Ὀδυσῆα·
sentences.l: and dreadfully he shouted, urging on Odysseus:
sentences.i: and he shouted dreadfully, urging on Odysseus:
sentences.n: Diomedes calls to another man. σμερδαλέον is the neuter adjective used as an adverb, ‘dreadfully’; ἐβόησεν is the aorist of βοάω ‘shout’, and ἐποτρύνων the participle of ἐποτρύνω ‘urge on’. Ὀδυσῆα is the epic accusative of Ὀδυσσεύς.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ
πῇ φεύγεις μετὰ νῶτα βαλὼν κακὸς ὣς ἐν ὁμίλῳ;
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
where do you flee, having turned your back, like a base man in the throng?
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, where are you fleeing, with your back turned, like a base man in the throng?
sentences.n: Diomedes’ speech begins with Odysseus’ full address, the vocative διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ, whose English is kept. πῇ φεύγεις is ‘where do you flee?’; μετὰ νῶτα βαλών is ‘having turned your back’, literally ‘thrown your back (to the rear)’. κακὸς ὣς is ‘like a base man’ (κακός ‘base, cowardly’), and ἐν ὁμίλῳ is ‘in the throng’. The unit ends with the Greek question mark, which is the semicolon. Diomedes’ speech begins.

sentences.t: μή τίς τοι φεύγοντι μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ πήξῃ·
sentences.l: lest someone, as you flee, fix a spear in your back;
sentences.i: lest someone fix a spear in your back as you flee;
sentences.n: μή τις … πήξῃ is ‘lest anyone fix’, a warning with μή and the aorist subjunctive of πήγνυμι ‘fix’. τοι φεύγοντι is ‘you as you flee’, a dative of the person affected, and μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ is ‘a spear in the back’, with ἐν after its noun and μετάφρενον the back between the shoulders. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μέν’ ὄφρα γέροντος ἀπώσομεν ἄγριον ἄνδρα.
sentences.l: but stay, so that from the old man we may thrust off the fierce man.
sentences.i: but stand firm, so that we may drive the fierce man away from the old man.
sentences.n: μέν’ is the imperative μένε of μένω, ‘stay, stand firm’. ὄφρα … ἀπώσομεν is a purpose clause with the short-vowel subjunctive of ἀπωθέω, ‘thrust off’, so ‘so that we may thrust away’. γέροντος is ‘from the old man’, Nestor, in the genitive of separation, and ἄγριον ἄνδρα is ‘the fierce man’, that is Hector, unnamed. Diomedes’ speech runs on into the next part.
